claims.text: Formation and crystal-structure selection in noble-metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles are governed by the interplay between rapid thermal kinetics and atomic diffusion.
Excessively rapid heating and cooling provide insufficient time for constituent atoms to diffuse and homogenize.
Insufficient diffusion during rapid thermal processing causes phase separation and elemental segregation.
Insufficient diffusion during rapid thermal processing causes irregular nanoparticle morphology.
Reducing heating and cooling rates increases the time available for atomic diffusion.
Longer diffusion times enhance atomic mixing in noble-metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Enhanced interdiffusion reduces local concentration gradients that promote segregation and competing-phase nucleation.
Slower thermal ramps allow the system to overcome kinetic barriers that otherwise lock in metastable multiphase structures.
Atomic-scale mixing and diffusion length determine whether a uniform single phase or a phase-separated structure emerges.
A moderated thermal ramp will produce a more homogeneous single-phase crystal structure than a rapid-heating and rapid-cooling baseline.
A moderated thermal ramp will improve control of nanoparticle morphology.
A moderated thermal ramp will lower the tendency for high-temperature thermal decomposition.
Improved single-phase formation will be observable through sharper XRD peaks and more consistent TEM elemental maps.
Single-phase formation can depend on a high-temperature processing window.
The proposed ramp-rate mechanism applies to noble-metal alloys containing more than five elements near a temperature where nucleation competes with diffusion.
The hypothesis may not apply when phase separation is controlled by thermodynamically incompatible elemental mixing.
The ramp-rate threshold separating single-phase and multiphase outcomes varies with the particular elemental combination.
